Best globe-trotting books & movies

Hi, friend!

Today, we're setting off on a globe-trotting adventure—no passport required! From far-flung destinations to journeys that cross continents, these books, movies, and shows bring the thrill of discovery straight to your screen and reading list.

Watch It, Read It

Around the World in Eighty Days

Streaming on Prime Video with PBS

David Tennant stars as a cautious English gentleman who wagers that he can circle the globe in just 80 days. Watch the colorful eight-episode series, then return to Jules Verne's classic novel for the story that first sent readers racing across continents.

10 TV Shows That Will Inspire You to Travel the World

Booked for Adventure

The 100-Year-Old Man Who Climbed Out the Window and Disappeared

by Jonas Jonasson

On his 100th birthday, Allan Karlsson decides to skip the party, climb out of his nursing home window, and see where the road takes him. What follows is a wildly funny adventure involving criminals, a suitcase full of cash, and a century's worth of unbelievable memories spanning the globe.

Lies and Weddings

by Kevin Kwan

From the author of Crazy Rich Asians comes a must-read globe-trotting rom-com! When a lavish wedding on the Big Island of Hawaii goes spectacularly off course, old secrets, complicated romances and family expectations come crashing together.

Trailer of the Day

Matchbox: The Movie

The lives of childhood friends get thrown into overdrive when their long-missing former leader, Sean (John Cena)—now an undercover CIA agent—pulls them into a frantic international mission to save the world. Also starring Jessica Biel, Sam Richardson, Teyonah Parris and Arturo Castro. Streaming October 9 on Apple TV.

Shows to restore your faith in humanity

Hey, friend!

The Little League World Series is officially underway, which is the one moment every summer when our faith in humanity is collectively restored as we watch kids from different cultures around the world unite over competition and a love for baseball. In keeping with that theme, we've curated the best feel-good coming-of-age shows, the books that prove sports teach lessons no classroom ever could, and the underdog movies that need to be on your watchlist.

Coming-of-Age Shows to Restore Your Faith in Humanity

Nothing will make you optimistic for the future like watching teens overcoming adversity to become the best version of themselves. These are the series that do it best.

The Crossover

Twin basketball phenoms Josh and JB Bell are inseparable until growing up starts pulling them in different directions, on the court and off. Kwame Alexander adapts his own Newbery-winning novel, with Sean Patrick Thomas as their father, a former pro player adjusting to life after the NBA. It's the rare sports show that's also an uplifting family watch.

More Than a Game: Books About What Sports Actually Teach Us

In many of the best sports books, the game itself is almost beside the point. They use the sport as a way in, and what they're really writing about is everything that happens off the field.

The Art of Fielding

by Chad Harbach

Henry Skrimshander is a gifted shortstop who seems destined for big league stardom, until one wild throw shatters his confidence. Chad Harbach spent a decade writing his debut novel, which reads less like a sports book and more like a campus story about ambition, identity, and the fear of losing the one thing you counted on.

Long Shots: The Best Underdog Sports Movies

Everyone loves watching a team nobody believes in prove the haters wrong. Here are the underdog films you need to add to your watchlist.

The Mighty Ducks

A disgraced lawyer sentenced to community service must coach the worst pee-wee hockey team in Minnesota. Emilio Estevez spends the season turning a group of misfits who can't stay upright on skates into a team that actually believes in itself. It may not be a baseball movie, but it's the perfect story to pair with the Little League World Series.

End of summer adventure movies and books

Hi, friend!

Summer may be winding down, but there's still time to squeeze in one or two more adventures. Whether you're adventuring outdoors, escaping into a great book, or soaking up peak summer vibes from home, these picks are all about making the most of the season before fall takes over.

One Last Summer Adventure

Before the season slips away, head outside—at least from the comfort of your couch—with two movies about trading the everyday for a little wilderness, freedom, and adventure.

A Walk in the Woods

Streaming on Prime Video

Robert Redford and Nick Nolte hit the Appalachian Trail in this buddy comedy as two old friends attempting an ambitious trek they may be wildly underprepared for. The scenery is gorgeous and the mishaps are plentiful.

The Kings of Summer

Streaming on Paramount+

Three teenage friends decide to ditch their parents, build a house in the woods, and spend the summer living entirely on their own terms. What follows is a funny, offbeat coming-of-age adventure packed with friendship, freedom, and the kind of endless-summer energy worth squeezing in while you still can.

Binge-Worthy Shows With Peak Summer Vibes

If you're holding onto that summer feeling, escape with these iconic shows!

Make the Most of the Journey

There's still time for one more adventure, even if it starts on the page.

The Kicking the Bucket List

by Cathy Hopkins

When three estranged sisters reunite after their mother's death, they discover she's left them one final challenge: complete her bucket list together before they can receive their inheritance. Funny, heartfelt, and full of unexpected detours.

The Unlikely Pilgrimage of Harold Fry

by Rachel Joyce

Harold Fry steps out to mail a letter and, on impulse, just keeps walking, setting off on a hundreds-of-miles journey across England to visit an old friend. Along the way, his spontaneous trek becomes a moving story about hope, regret, connection, and what can happen when you decide it's not too late to take the long way.

Hey, friend!

This week marks the premiere of Season 18 of It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia, stretching its reign as the longest-running live-action sitcom in American TV history! In its honor, we've curated the best entertainment to pair with it: the 10 most iconic American sitcoms of all time, the best books with morally bankrupt protagonists, and the movies that got Philly right.

Comedy Hall of Fame: The 10 Best American Sitcoms of All Time

Every generation gets a handful of sitcoms that people are still quoting years later. These are the ten that will be remembered forever, from the studio era through streaming.

It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia

Charlie, Dennis, Mac, Dee, and Frank are awful people who have spent two decades running the worst bar in Philadelphia. Rob McElhenney, Glenn Howerton, and Charlie Day created the show as a $200 proof-of-concept in 2005, and now it's the longest-running live-action sitcom in American TV history. Season 18 is out now!

Bad to the Bone: Books With Morally Bankrupt Protagonists

ISAIP leans into our fascination with unlikeable main characters, even if they're not as reprehensible as these literary monsters.

Filth

by Irvine Welsh

Bruce Robertson is arguably fiction's most irredeemable character. He's a corrupt, drug-fueled Edinburgh detective who spends more energy sabotaging his colleagues than solving the murder case in front of him. Irvine Welsh's 1998 novel, narrated in part by a literal tapeworm living inside Bruce, is a dark and captivating satire.

Brotherly Love: The Best Movies Set in Philadelphia

Before Paddy's Pub, Philadelphia already had a cinematic identity of its own. These are the movies that captured the city's grit and attitude.

Rocky

A broke, small-time boxer from South Philly gets a once-in-a-lifetime shot at the heavyweight title and turns training into a citywide event. Sylvester Stallone wrote the script in three days and refused to sell it unless he could star. To this day, tourists from around the world visit the steps outside The Art Museum because of Rocky Balboa.

The end of one of Netflix's biggest shows

Hi, friend!

I almost never binge-watch shows. I can only think of a handful of instances when I've watched a whole series in a day: skipping class in college to binge Season 1 of Goliath, watching Tiger King with my dad during the height of the COVID lockdowns, and crying to Normal People with my fiancée on a rainy Sunday.

So when I say I binged 9 episodes of Game of Thrones on Sunday, that should tell you how much I'm loving the show. And before you ask, yes, it's my first time watching. I may be 15 years late to this iconic series, but as they say: Better late than never! I've heard plenty of discourse around the botched series finale, so I want your opinion: Is Game of Thrones Season 8 worth watching? Or should I skip it entirely? Reply to this email to let me know!

Studio Ghibli veterans Akihiko Yamashita and Shinji Otsuka handle animation on this devastating adaptation of Machiko Kyo's manga.

posts.text:
The joy of the unexpected — Wellness Pix

August 18 is Serendipity Day! We're celebrating the unexpected turns, chance encounters, and little surprises that can lead us somewhere better than we planned. From rediscovering yourself to finding connection in unlikely places, these picks are a reminder to leave a little room for the good you didn't see coming.

Read It, Watch It

Where'd You Go, Bernadette
by Maria Semple

Sometimes the best path forward is the one you never planned on taking. Where'd You Go, Bernadette follows one woman's unexpected journey back to herself and the daughter determined to find her. Read Maria Semple's witty, heartfelt novel, then watch Cate Blanchett bring Bernadette's creative comeback to life onscreen.

Lost & Found & the Unexpected

These two warmhearted novels are full of chance connections that prove something unexpected can lead you exactly where you need to be.

The Keeper of Lost Things
by Ruth Hogan

Anthony Peardew has spent years collecting lost objects and carefully cataloging each one. When his assistant Laura inherits his collection, she takes on his unfinished mission to reunite the objects with their owners—and discovers friendships and new possibilities along the way.

The Authenticity Project
by Clare Pooley

It starts with a small green notebook in which one lonely artist writes the truth about his life, then leaves it for someone else to find. As the notebook passes from stranger to stranger, their honest confessions spark unexpected friendships, community, and even romance. It's a feel-good story about what can happen when we keep ourselves open to new connections.

Now Streaming

The Dink

Jake Johnson stars as Dusty Boyd, a former tennis prodigy whose life takes an unexpected turn when he gets pulled into the fast-growing world of pickleball. Produced by Ben Stiller, this underdog comedy serves up rivalry, second chances, and plenty of laughs—a fitting reminder that sometimes the detour you never saw coming is exactly where the fun begins. Streaming on Apple TV.

Must-watch films to celebrate Elvis Week
posts.text:
Hey, friend!

Did you know it’s currently Elvis Week? This annual week-long celebration of the “King of Rock & Roll” takes place every year in Memphis, Tennessee. Since most of us won’t be visiting the world-famous Graceland estate anytime soon, we decided to round up the best Elvis movies and docs, reads on rock 'n' roll's golden age, and the decade’s greatest musical biopics to help you celebrate from the comfort of your couch.

Long Live the King: The Best Elvis Movies & Docs

From the iconic sequined jumpsuits in Vegas to grainy archival footage of a 21-year-old kid at Sun Records, these are the movies and docs that show the man behind the music.

Elvis

Baz Luhrmann's fever-dream biopic tracks Elvis's rise and unraveling through the eyes of Colonel Tom Parker (Tom Hanks), the manager who built him into a phenomenon and profited off every moment of it. Austin Butler masterfully disappears into the role—so much so that his real-life voice still has hints of Elvis’s to this day.

Backstage Pass: Books Exploring the Golden Age of Rock 'n' Roll

Movies give you the highlight reel, but these books shine a light on everything that got left out: the label politics, the bad contracts, and the moments nobody put on film.

Last Train to Memphis

by Peter Guralnick

The first half of Peter Guralnick's two-volume Elvis biography covers his life from birth through 1958, before the Army, before Vegas, and before his songs took over the world. It's considered the definitive account of how rock 'n' roll began, treating Presley as a working musician rather than a myth.

Top 10 Musical Biopics of the Decade

Once Elvis Week comes to an end, here are 10 more must-watch musical biopics worth singing along to.

Respect

Aretha Franklin handpicked Jennifer Hudson to play her years before this film got made, and it's easy to see why once Hudson opens her mouth. The story tracks Franklin's rise from her father's church choir to international stardom.

posts.title: Must-watch films to celebrate Elvis Week
posts.text:
Hey, friend!

Did you know it’s currently Elvis Week? This annual week-long celebration of the “King of Rock & Roll” takes place every year in Memphis, Tennessee. Since most of us won’t be visiting the world-famous Graceland estate anytime soon, we decided to round up the best Elvis movies and docs, reads on rock 'n' roll's golden age, and the decade’s greatest musical biopics to help you celebrate from the comfort of your couch.

Long Live the King: The Best Elvis Movies & Docs

From the iconic sequined jumpsuits in Vegas to grainy archival footage of a 21-year-old kid at Sun Records, these are the movies and docs that show the man behind the music.

Elvis

Baz Luhrmann's fever-dream biopic tracks Elvis's rise and unraveling through the eyes of Colonel Tom Parker (Tom Hanks), the manager who built him into a phenomenon and profited off every moment of it. Austin Butler masterfully disappears into the role—so much so that his real-life voice still has hints of Elvis’s to this day.

Backstage Pass: Books Exploring the Golden Age of Rock 'n' Roll

Movies give you the highlight reel, but these books shine a light on everything that got left out: the label politics, the bad contracts, and the moments nobody put on film.

Last Train to Memphis

by Peter Guralnick

The first half of Peter Guralnick's two-volume Elvis biography covers his life from birth through 1958, before the Army, before Vegas, and before his songs took over the world. It's considered the definitive account of how rock 'n' roll began, treating Presley as a working musician rather than a myth.

Top 10 Musical Biopics of the Decade

Once Elvis Week comes to an end, here are 10 more must-watch musical biopics worth singing along to.

Respect

Aretha Franklin handpicked Jennifer Hudson to play her years before this film got made, and it's easy to see why once Hudson opens her mouth. The story tracks Franklin's rise from her father's church choir to international stardom.

posts.title: “An epic love story... a gorgeously written novel”
posts.text:
Hi, friend!

Welcome back to Insider Pix, where we uncover what entertainment and culture insiders are watching, reading, and listening to! Next up:

Leigh Haber

Leigh Haber is a seasoned publishing executive who spent a decade overseeing Oprah’s Book Club and book coverage for O Magazine and Oprah Daily, where she served as VP, Books. Her wide-ranging career has included roles as an editor, publicity director, producer, speechwriter, and book reviewer, and she has worked with authors including Al Gore, Steve Martin, Terry Gross, and Alice Walker. She now joins Sourcebooks as VP, Executive Director of Communications and Special Projects.

Leigh’s 5 Picks

A 5-star-worthy book you’d recommend to anyone?

The Loneliness of Sonia and Sunny by Kiran Desai. Yes, it’s 700-something pages, but it’s an epic love story alongside a portrait of alienation and displacement—a gorgeously written novel by the Booker Prize-winning author of The Inheritance of Loss.

Best TV show you’ve watched recently?

It’s a tie between Hacks and The Comeback. Hacks is hilarious—the relationship between its two stars is so complex and electric. Jean Smart is a genius. And The Comeback is off-kilter in a way that is so Lisa Kudrow. Riveting.

Best movie you watched recently?

Michael, starring Jaafar Jackson. I know there will be haters for this choice, but I couldn’t take my eyes off the screen. Jaafar’s performance was off the charts, and I’d forgotten how great the music is.

A hidden gem you wish more people knew about?

The film Juliet, Naked. Starring Rose Byrne, Ethan Hawke, and Chris O’Dowd—I love its quirky warmth.

Go-to weekly podcast?

Good Hang with Amy Poehler. She’s like the embodiment of fun. Takes me out of my head. That episode with Will Ferrell?? Awkward and hilarious.

Pix: What is the best book you’ve read so far this year, and what made it stand out?

“LH: It’s a tie between The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout and Whistler by Ann Patchett. I didn’t want either of them to end.”

Pix: You spent over a decade as the Director of Oprah’s Book Club. Is there a particular Oprah's Book Club selection or author that holds a special place in your heart, and what makes it so memorable?

“LH: I can narrow it down to three. An American Marriage by Tayari Jones is one. I’d loved Tayari’s Silver Sparrow but wasn’t able to get Oprah to select it, so when An American Marriage came out, I was all over it. And Tayari is a delight. We picked The Underground Railroad by Colson Whitehead, and that was before he won the Pulitzer. Very proud of that one. And then Caste by Isabel Wilkerson. I think those who read it with us began to view racism in a completely different way.”

Pix: If you could host a dream dinner party with three authors—dead or alive—who's getting an invitation and why?

“LH: Toni Morrison, for sure. I adore her fiction, but she was also such a great essayist and thinker. She would preside over the dinner party, in my fantasy. (and of course Oprah did hold a dinner party on camera with her…) Amor Towles would have to be there, because he’s such a classic gentleman and I love his white suits. And I’d have to go with Toni Cade Bambara as our third. She and Toni were friends and colleagues, and TCB is such an underrated writer. She also had a sparkling personality–radiated warmth and humor.”

Pix: You are the director of The Ink Book Club, which has a call to action for all bibliophiles: “In this era of book banning, be fierce!” If you could put a banned book into every reader’s hands, which would you pick and why?

“LH: The 1619 Project, by Nikole Hannah-Jones. We have to start looking at our country’s history more realistically if we are going to move forward in a productive way.”

The most chilling true crime shows of 2026 — Today's Pix

Earlier this summer, Netflix's Maternal Instinct had everyone talking about its chilling depiction of a real COVID-era case. Now, a new season of Conversations with a Killer is landing this week. With the genre having a killer lineup this summer, we've rounded up the most fascinating true crime stories across TV, podcasts, and books.

THE MOST CHILLING TRUE CRIME SHOWS OF THE YEAR (SO FAR)
True crime TV isn't just popular right now, it's absolutely dominating. These are the new shows that made viewers stay up way past their bedtime, one creepy episode at a time.
Conversations with a Killer: The Charles Manson Tapes — Joe Berlinger's docuseries returns for a new volume, tracing Charles Manson's rise as a cult leader through unreleased prison recordings, firsthand accounts, and archival footage most viewers have never seen. It's the franchise's darkest season yet, and the closest anyone's gotten to hearing Manson explain himself in his own words. Only on Netflix August 12.

NEW & UNSETTLING TRUE CRIME PODCASTS
From mysterious cold cases to shocking family secrets nobody saw coming, the best true crime podcasts of the year prove the genre still has new angles to explore.
The Idiot — For years, M. Gessen wrote about the world's worst people: dictators, terrorists, human rights abusers. Then their own cousin Allen got arrested for trying to have his ex-wife killed. Serial Productions' latest is the studio's funniest true crime podcast yet, and its most personal.

PAGE-TURNERS: THE MOST ADDICTIVE TRUE CRIME BOOKS OF 2026
The best true crime writing turns real tragedy into something you can't put down without ever losing the human stakes.
London Falling by Patrick Radden Keefe — Patrick Radden Keefe, the writer behind Say Nothing and Empire of Pain, tells the story of a London teenager who invented an entire identity as a Russian oligarch's son before he was found dead in the Thames. This devastating and spellbinding read is easily one of the biggest books of the year.

August is kind of a weird month: summer isn't over, fall hasn't started, and everyone is scrambling to take a few more days of vacation. So why not lean into the weirdness? Today's books are delightfully off-kilter, with a bloody Hollywood tale, some multiverse romance, and more.

FANTASY SPOTLIGHT — Dreamland by Olivie Blake
New York Times bestselling author Olivie Blake (The Atlas Six, Girl Dinner) returns with a bloody good novel about an aspiring actress who is drawn into the orbit of a powerful Hollywood dynasty, as a seductive heir and her own ambition threaten to consume her. Alix E. Harrow (Starling House) raves: "This is Olivie Blake at the height of her power, doing cartwheels on the high wire. Dreamland is a sweat-slick Hollywood fable about fame, fortune, and the sins we'd commit for either. A gory, gothic masterpiece."

ROMANCE SPOTLIGHT — In What World by Bridget Morrissey
In this "true love letter to theatre kids and queer folks" (Hannah Bonam-Young), two former high school rivals begrudgingly reunite to find their missing drama teacher, only to tumble through a series of alternate realities where other versions of themselves are much more honest about their feelings for each other. Equal parts multiverse adventure and simmering second-chance romance, this clever, heartfelt novel asks what happens when the person you can't stand might be the person you can't live without.

"A rare and beautifully controlled novel of magic, intrigue, and obsession…. Delightful and dangerous. A feat of marvelous showmanship!" —Rachel Beanland, author of This House Is on Fire

Today's Book Pix is delightfully unhinged. From an NSFW rabbit hole to a shipwreck-fueled family drama, Karin Slaughter's newest page-turner, and a literary classic getting a very modern adaptation, today's picks are guaranteed to keep you on your toes.

IS SENTIENT OBJECT SMUT HAVING A MOMENT?
As my colleagues and I cackled over all the early Wicker memes, I felt the need to point out that sentient object smut is an actual romance subgenre. And just like Wicker, they frequently serve a hefty dose of humor along with their spice.
Unhinged by Vera Valentine — In this paranormal romance, a woman must trust the sentient front door that's secretly protected her for years when a deadly stalker threatens her life. As odd as it may sound, this book has a cult following: more than 10k reviews on Amazon and almost 30k on Goodreads. The door is actually a dryad shifter who gets stuck in door form, so there's a Greek mythology angle. Readers agree it is totally bonkers, yet somehow completely delightful.

THE BIG DEBUT — The Responsible Party by Claire Carusillo
When a modern-day scandal and a decades-old murder collide, a canceled skincare influencer uncovers the wild history of the "unsinkable" women who came before her. Vulture calls this debut about an unforgettable family "pleasurably busy and delightfully odd," while The New York Times hails it as "a rollicking, hilarious tale of shipwreck, shenanigans and murder."

THRILLER SPOTLIGHT — The Secrets We Hide by Karin Slaughter

Expect buried secrets, mounting suspicions, and plenty of twists as Clifton and her sister unravel what really happened to the Vickery family one terrible night. Freida McFadden: "Few writers can balance pulse-pounding suspense and emotional truth as brilliantly as Karin Slaughter."

PAGE TO SCREEN — My Brilliant Career
A 125-year-old novel is getting a very 2026 glow-up. Premiering August 13 on Netflix, My Brilliant Career gives Miles Franklin's 1901 classic a wildly modern makeover, following aspiring writer Sybylla Melvyn (Philippa Northeast) as she chooses creative ambition over marriage and society's expectations in early 20th-century Australia. Created by an all-female team of writers, producers, and directors.

3 Irish picks you’re missing out on

Welcome back to Insider Pix, where we uncover what entertainment and culture insiders are watching, reading, and listening to! Next up:

Dermot McCormack

Dermot McCormack is a transformational CEO, President, and investor with a track record of scaling media, streaming, and technology companies through bold strategy, operational excellence, and creative disruption. Today, he is CEO and Founder of Bravo Mondo, a growth-stage advisory and investment firm.

Dermot’s 5 Picks

A 5-star-worthy book you’d recommend to anyone?

The Undoing Project by Michael Lewis

Best movie you watched recently?

Good Luck, Have Fun, Don’t Die (now streaming on Hulu)

Best TV show you’ve watched recently?

The Dry from RTE & ITV

A hidden gem you wish more people knew about?

Probably not a hidden gem but Desert Island Discs from the BBC. They put all episodes for over 30 years or more up as a podcast. It’s basically your favorite songs and a book and one item you would bring to a desert island.

Go-to weekly podcast?

Raging Moderates with Scott Gallaoway & Jessica Tarlov

Pix: Having been born and raised in Dublin, what are your top 3 picks of Irish media that you think every American should check out?

DM: Music: Glen Hansard

Movie: In Bruges, starring Colin Farrell and Brendan Gleeson

TV show: The Dry

Pix: What's one piece of entertainment—whether it's a documentary, podcast, or book—that you think every entrepreneur should experience, and why?

DM: If you are an entrepreneur or starting a company of any type, please read Shoe Dog by Phil Knight about the story of Nike…and then don’t do it!! Just kidding.

Pix: You've spent your career at the intersection of media and technology. What's one entertainment trend you're genuinely excited about right now?

DM: I’m working on several projects that blend the physical and digital in terms of narrative. Think immersive or experiential (although we need better words). Because a whole generation has been doing less and less in the physical world, I think entertainment will step in and fill some of this gap but be blended with new digital experiences. Think the Sphere, Cosm, or Outernet in London! This is a really exiting and fun trend in my view.

Pix: Looking back at your MTV and digital media days, what was the first moment that made you realize the way people consumed entertainment was fundamentally changing? How have those experiences shaped the way you think about AI in entertainment today?

DM: I think when Lost was the first show that came out and you could buy episodes from iTunes for your Mac and iPod! It was the first show I watched solely in a non-traditional TV environment. It also just happens to be an awesome show. I would watch on planes!

What it tells me about AI in entertainment today is, first of all, the entertainment had to be great. No amount of technology will make a bad story into a great story (yet). In the Lost example, technology gave the audience more choice for content and flexibility on how, when, and where you could watch. Hopefully, AI will allow new stories from new voices in ways we could never imagine and will democratize who gets to make what. There will also be some bad effects that I assume, if you are reading this, you can imagine. I’m hopeful the good will outweigh the bad, and I think the journey is just beginning and like all revolutions, it will be bumpy!!

By day, Bruce Wayne is a Gotham City billionaire. By night, he's Batman, patrolling a city crawling with costumed criminals who are just as damaged as he is. With Season 2 of Batman: Caped Crusader premiering on Friday, now's the perfect time for a rewatch!

Before Tom Holland ever put on the suit, one movie made Peter Parker a household name, and it still holds up over twenty years later.

Spider-Man

A shy teenager gets bitten by a genetically modified spider and quickly learns that with great power comes great responsibility. "My favorite restaurant in the entire world" — Insider Pix

Welcome back to Insider Pix, where we uncover what entertainment and culture insiders are watching, reading, and listening to! Next up:

Molly Sterrs

After more than two decades working in food and hospitality, Molly Sterrs now brings an industry insider's eye to her writing about food, beverage, and the people shaping the region's dining culture for Edible Manhattan's group of publications. Based in the Hudson Valley, she is particularly interested in food media, local history, and the strange, specific stories hiding behind menus, restaurants, and the things people love to eat.

Molly's 5 Picks

A hidden gem you wish more people knew about?

Good Eats with Alton Brown. It was integral to my childhood/adolescence because it taught me not only how to cook, but why certain cooking methods worked. Food TV used to trust viewers to be curious; now, so much of it has been gamified and cartoonified into something I find incredibly boring. Alton Brown made people care enough about their food to want to understand it, cook it well, and enjoy it properly. I miss shows like that.

Best TV show you've watched recently?

Anne Rice's The Vampire Lestat (season three of Interview with the Vampire). It's trashy, wildly campy, and the acting is far better than anything this gloriously over the top show has a right to be.

Best movie you watched recently?

The Devil's Rain. Ernest Borgnine is a perfect little satanic freak in it, the cast is bizarrely stacked, and the whole movie is exactly the kind of strange, gooey 1970s horror I love.

A 5-star-worthy book you'd recommend to anyone?

A Prayer for Owen Meany by John Irving. At its center is a lifelong friendship between the narrator and Owen, a tiny boy with a permanently damaged voice who believes he knows exactly how and when he'll die. It's a funny, infuriating, heartbreaking novel about faith, fate, and the people who permanently rearrange your life. I find myself returning to it every few years, and I get something new out of it with each revisit.

Go-to weekly podcast?

Woo Woo with Rachel Dratch. It hits the perfect sweet spot between paranormal storytelling and comedy, with celebrity guests sharing their strangest encounters. As a host, Rachel is curious without being credulous and skeptical without ruining the fun, which is exactly how I like my woo-woo.

Pix: What cookbook has earned a permanent spot on your shelf?

MS: It's a tie between Every Day Is Saturday by Sarah Copeland and The Food Lab by J. Kenji López-Alt. Copeland's recipes are incredibly accessible but still beautiful and impressive, whether you're feeding a crowd or just your family on a random Tuesday. Nothing is particularly flashy or mind-blowing, which is exactly what I like about it. The Food Lab feeds my endless curiosity about the hows and whys of cooking, much like Good Eats did when I was growing up.

Pix: If logistics were no obstacle, what dishes are you including in your hypothetical final meal?

MS: I want chicken Francese from literally anywhere because I've never had a bad version, New England clam chowder from the dearly departed Cappy's Chowder House in Camden, ME, a Cali carnitas burrito from And Breakfast Burritos in San Diego, and ribs from Jack's Bar-B-Que in Nashville. I'd also need my mom's pot roast with red cabbage, schnitzel from Mountain Brauhaus in Gardiner, NY, banoffee ice cream from Fortunes in Tivoli, NY, and whatever is being served at the monthly Persian feast at Brushland Eating House in Bovina, NY—my favorite restaurant in the entire world.

Pix: Is there a restaurant dish you've had this year that you can't stop thinking about?

MS: The biscuits and gravy at Jax Diner in Portsmouth, RI. I stopped there on the way home from a wedding in Providence after plans to visit a nearby IHOP fell through, which now feels like divine intervention. The place is tiny, the menu is exactly as expansive as a diner menu should be, and everything is made in-house. I would love nothing more than to drown myself in their perfectly peppered sausage gravy.

Groundhog Day meets Practical Magic in this "fun and sexy" (People) new novel from the author of The Other Side of Now. Four estranged friends reunite to settle the will of the woman who shaped their teenage summers, only to find themselves trapped in an endless weekend that forces them to confront the secrets that tore them apart. Grab the tissues, but don't forget your sense of humor, because this one balances grief with big laughs against a deliciously summery coastal backdrop.

HISTORICAL FANTASY SPOTLIGHT

Henry Tudor Must Die
by Jillian Laine

What if Henry VIII's wives got the last laugh? This wickedly entertaining fantasy reunites Anne Boleyn, Catherine of Aragon, and the rest of Henry VIII's legendary queens for a magical revenge mission. Sharp, bloody, and outrageously fun, it's pure wish-fulfillment for history lovers and fans of the musical Six. As Emily Krempholtz puts it: "Henry Tudor Must Die is an exquisite declaration of female rage, sisterhood, and what it takes to stand against the abuse of power in a deeply unjust world."
